## 3. Movies about people struggling to be good

**Score:** 17
**Body:** I have been recently coming to terms with the fact that I have spent a lot of my life acting like a terrible person, and have hurt a lot of people unintentionally.  I just lost two people who meant a lot to me because of it.

I think it would help me to see a story about characters that are flawed but not inherently bad, who have hurt people due to their own mental illness. I want to try to reflect on myself as much as I can. are there any movies you guys know of that touch on this topic in a nuanced way?

One of the only ones that has helped me in this way is perks of being a wallflower, although Charlie isn’t a terrible person or anything he definitely hurt his friends as a result of his own issues. What are some other movies that show a character being hated but don’t paint them in an evil light?

Edit: thank you all for your suggestions :) I’d like to add that I’m looking for things that are more based around personal and complicated relationships between friends, and less about being a general bad person (like Groundhog Day although that’s a great movie). The movie as you are is a good example, the tv show girls works even, all of those guys suck. Or movies about someone trying to redeem themselves in a personal sense, like good will hunting. ## 3. What Is A Perfect Movie?

**Score:** 106
**Body:** A movie, technically, is the visual presentation of a story, or an episode of it, that aims to immerse its audience in its virtual word and forces them to engage with its characters and underlying ideas. A great movie then is one which can fulfill its aim to a high standard. A perfect movie fulfills those standards to a degree which makes it resonate with the soul, mind, and deepest emotions of its contemporaries as well as posterity. In my opinion, the basic components of a movie are the following,

1. **Narrative/Plot**: the significance & depth of its underlying story/philosophy and how well constructed and delivered it is.
2. **Character**: the presentation, development, and  psychological makeup of the characters that drive the narrative. How well do they embody the essence of the movie and how it manifests in their dialogues and actions.
3. **Casting**: the physical, emotional, and intellectual congruity of the assigned actor to his character.
4. **Cinematography**: how well selected, constructed, coordinated and complementary the setting, camera work, imagery, and composition are to the narrative. And how aesthetic and immersive they are.

The degree to which the above components are constructed, blended, and optimized determines the excellence of a certain movie. Some movies which I deem to have excelled in these respects are: **Cure** (1997) , **The Shawshank Redemption** (1994), **No Country for Old Men** (2007), **Memories of Murder** (2003), **The Banshees of Inisherin** (2022), **The Chaser** (2008), **There Will be Blood** (2007), **Oldboy** (2003), **Seven** (1995), **The Wailing** (2016), **The Grand Budapest Hotel** (2014), **Stalker** (1979), **12 Angry Men** (1957).

What are your perfect movies? And any recommendations?

## 5. You can see everything was incredible but…

**Body:** I was blown away by you can see everything and left the movie with a much different view of Holmes than I was expecting. She’s delusional but maybe not malicious.” I even thought that maybe she was autistic and an unintentional compulsive liar. (My best friend in high school had Asperger’s and was a compulsive liar but she never lied about anything important and was a very funny and kind person she just didn’t know how to respond in social situations so would make up stories that were funny and entertaining but not true) 

WELL… the movie also left me curious to learn more and so I listened to the bad blood podcast by the journalist who initially exposed her and oh my god she’s so so so much worse than I ever imagined. She absolutely knew what she was doing and didn’t care how many people got hurt or could have died as a result of her actions. She knew the machines couldn’t do all the tests she said and yet she deployed them to millions of REAL SICK PEOPLE who could have and may have died because the results were inaccurate. She also drove whistle blowers to suicide by burying them in legal debt when they tried to stand up for patient safety. 

I know many people already knew this going in but I really wish the documentary had included some of her blatant lies and how they endangered people’s lives because the documentary kind of makes her a little sympathetic which I think was her whole goal in the first place. She may have genuinely been abused by sunny and her new husband but that doesn’t change the fact that she was an active participant in this and many of the texts from the trial actually show that sunny tried to hold her back from some of the bigger lies. She deserves to be in prison for a long time.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I do not understand Robert Eggers’s dislike of The Witch (2015)

**Score:** 251
**Body:** Everybody of course has a little bit of cringe at their early creative endeavours — but if you do some research, you will see that there is a lot of evidence to show Eggers finds The Witch near impossible to watch. His directors commentary on YouTube (https://youtu.be/K6FoU\_CYlAg?si=b7hguxljhexZXRsk) kind of explains it — he seems very bogged down in extremely obscure historical details that only he and like two anthropologists would ever notice, and a handful of shots/frames that he (and really only he) says are imperfect.

And I don’t mean that he simply thinks it could be better (it would also be strange if he thought it was perfect, no notes) but he seems to think it’s basically trash that shouldn’t exist.

I point this out because The Witch is probably the most technically impressive debut feature in some time, and shows a great deal of control of process — other debuts, while good, often have flaws that even a layman would notice but forgive for being the first of something. The biggest sin The Witch commits according to its director is having the wrong kind of wood seams, and it’s a hanging offence.

The obvious answer is that he is a perfectionist, but IMO it’s not as if his later films necessarily blow it out of the water. I like a few of his movies but I find The Witch to be where he strikes a good balance between historical fidelity and an actual tangible character arc for the protagonist. A lot of his other movies don’t feel emotionally accessible in the same way. His perspective and great dislike for it is therefore interesting to me.

Anyway, posting it here for discussion. Agree or disagree, whatever.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Witch is a truly beloved movie by nearly everyone. 

Most directors intensely dislike watching their stuff because they only see the flaws and they remember they actually wanted *this* to happen but it rained that day so they had to settle for *that* instead. 

The only director I can remember that truly loves watching his own stuff is Tarantino. And the only actor I can recall that enjoys watching his own movies is Samuel L. Jackson. 

Most others just avoid it and it gets them in their own heads too much. 
  - Another actor who loved his movie was Andre the Giant. I realise that's not the same but his love for the Princess Bride is something that makes me happy to think about
  - I guarantee there are plenty of actors (and to a lesser extent, directors) who love to rewatch their own stuff. It's just something you can't openly admit to without coming across like a self-obsessed asshole.

It's hardly surprising Tarantino's the one guy that openly says it as, for all his talent, he's obsessed with his own mythology and is a massive naval gazer in general. And Sam Jackson is so cool he can get away with anything. 


    - Tarantino strikes me as an asshole so obsessed with himself that being known as a self-obsessed asshole is just sincerity.

https://clip.cafe/scott-pilgrim-vs-the-world-2010/somebody-bring-me-board/
2. There is a truly visceral rawness to The Witch where the other films he’s done have all had this sense of intentional artifice. He’s a filmmaker that always excites me but there is something very singular about The Witch that’s hard to beat 
  - Agree! The Witch feels dirty, and dreadful. It’s unsettling with every new scene. It’s an incredible HORROR movie (all caps), curious and yet familiar, personal, whereas his other works feel produced, detached, conceptual, but nonetheless excellent
  - I agree. All his later stuff feels "crafted" to some extent or other but the Witch just feels more...real. Like, those people were simply just overwhelmed by forces they couldn't comprehend--to me there's something very basic and terrifying about that. 
  - You've hit the nail on the head with this, I think it's part of the reason why I was disappointed by Nosferatu. On the one hand it could just be nothing more than a young(er) filmmaker finding his style but it does definitely feel a lot more "put on" in Nosferatu and The Northman. I'm still looking forward to Werwulf though because if nothing else they're always great entertainment
3. The Witch is the most original and has the most character and heart out of all his works. The rest have obviously been successful but since The Northman and his comments about how he feels he's improved his filmmaking I haven't felt any soul. Just more spectacle. 
4. I think it might also make sense exactly because its his debut, meaning he spent 10 years obsessively imagining all these details and building up this very precise vision of it.


Then he shoots it, has got to wing it and make all kinds of compromises, and now there is this discrepancy between his original imagination and the finished film that is gnawing at him.


With his later films he just doesnt have the time to develop that overdetailed imagination, so he actually starts relating to it more like any other director: A solid vision but then also happy to embrace whatever organically happens on set.


The thing is, both The Northman and Nosferatu I would say are actually worse in also exactly this issue he is so on about. As in elements of the set-design just being visibly a bit too clean and artificial to read as perfectly period-accurate.


Or rather, its on a level where even an amateur like me notices some of these things. Normally this wouldnt bother me in the slightest, but when you have his statements from the Witch in the back of your head, its just a bit confusing,  like "Ah, but *this* is ok now? I dont get it..."


I have to say to me it was actually highly surprising that he was able to switch gears so completely and become this very steady, productive director and producer. If you read his interviews on his process from The Witch I think you would have good reason to be sceptical that this guy could ever get a solid footing in hollywood. You would think that he is just a hopeless neurotic who will either take another 10 years to make his next movie, or go absolutely crazy when having to do the next movie under standard hollywood conditions.



I think the conclusion would be to see how he related to The Witch as indeed rather circumstantial. Its less "him" than maybe even he, himself thought. He was just this artist with no money and just his script that he thus spent 10 years over obsessing over every little detail over.


Then for his next films suddenly hollywood gave him bags of money, but also typical time-pressure, and he discovered that, no, this is actually not that intrinsic to him. He is perfectly happy and capable of just writing a story and getting it done on hollywoods terms, and not be that level of neurotic about it.

## 2. “Backrooms” has a great visual concept but not enough story

**Score:** 232
**Body:** I know I’m late to the party, but having now seen one of the most talked-about movies of the year, I sort of wish that Kane Parsons had a stronger script to work with in “Backrooms” because this was an impressive debut for a young director and, most of all, because the movie relies so heavily on his command of the visual concept.

I hear some found it boring, but I was fully invested. I found the atmosphere unsetting, and the unfamiliar logic of that place intriguing at first. I could almost feel some unknown presence around the corner. And then... the script took me out of it to focus on the characters’ pasts, their lingering trauma, their emotional issues, and the usual stuff you’d expect from a psychological horror movie with a therapist as one of the leads.

To be fair, for a story based on a web series based on a creepypasta, this one is better than it has to be. But the explicit connection between the Backrooms and the human mind gives the plot a misguided sense of self-importance (think “Being Charlie Kaufman”) without adding much psychological depth. And after the third or fourth fade to black to signal a character fainting or being knocked out, the difficulties of stretching such a thin premise to feature length became clear.

Since the visual concept is so powerful on its own, I felt that most of the creative decisions made to shape a more conventional plot weakened the mystery and narrowed the possibilities. That's how I see it, anyway.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I feel just the opposite.  I loved the movie, but I thought it would have been a better movie with far *less* explication.  Even in his YT series, I least liked the corporate aspect.   I like liminal spaces to be ambiguous, inscrutable.    I hate the obtrusive "it's about therapy and trauma!!!!!" overly didactic explication.   IMO  we should be left to interpret art, let it play over our feelings, and at times I feel the modern "it's about trauma!!!!" thing is basically someone tugging insistently on my sleeve and [telling me](https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/girl-explaining) the obvious didactic message.

As someone complained to me about this film a few days ago, "it's just about the vibes."  Well yes, most horror is about the vibes.   Horror isn't all the stabby-stabby part.   Fans are of course going to disagree on that, and with my opinion.   But I liked the vibes and aesthetics, and had to deliberately ignore the explication.
  - A better script and better plotting doesn't necessarily mean more exposition and direct explanation. I'd say it means the opposite. I don't think you an OP disagree.
  - Yeah it stumbles in the last 20-30 trying to explain stuff. Way cooler up to that. 
  - Oh, it wasn't really about trauma, though. It was about the often inconsistent and inaccurate histories we formulate for ourselves when we find ourselves in a present that we're unhappy with, whether it's trauma-based or not. Mary's past was traumatic, yes, but Clark's wasn't and he's simply in an undesirable mid-life situation due to his own mistakes and shortcomings that don't breach into the realm of trauma but are nevertheless the source of his depression. And so the backrooms become a projection of the 'loop' or 'maze' he builds for himself to justify his current state, that justification of course unreality, a distorted version of what we understand as the world. And the film really interestingly extrapolates this personal projection into a shared space where multiple people's personal mazes interact, grow, expand, and can be scientifically studied.

I thought it was a really interesting look at how we become our own unreliable narrators. And of course Captain Clark is essentially his own personal Minotaur, just as there was a Minotaur waiting for Will Navidson at the center of his personal labyrinth in House of Leaves, only Backrooms cleverly makes the Minotaur look like a monstrous version of everything Clark despises about his lot in life. And interestingly we never actually see the monster that attacks at the beginning and the post-credits scene, so are there multiple instances of 'personal demons' lurking in there? Now that Mary has interacted with the maze, is her mother in there now in some monstrous form, for instance?

I thought it was a great film. First 2/3 were genuinely creepy and then it dug in way deeper than I expected in the final act. It easily could have cruised along and just kept being creepy but it turned into a pretty interesting character study. Not saying it's perfect but it's way different, IMO, from films like The Babadook and Hereditary where "the real monster was our trauma all along". (Both of which are films I very much like, too.)
    - Exactly, I thought this was a pretty explicit interpretation of the Backrooms in the film ie, the Backrooms are an extradimensional manifestation of the human mind. Every time the mind recalls a memory, it is produced as a slight distortion of the original event, but never a 1:1 recreation. As time passes our ability to recall the event with accuracy diminishes; the location of a certain tree or a street is slightly off because we can't quite remember as well, or that memory became linked with another and becomes cross-contaminated, in a sense. So the Backrooms are layers of hundreds of millions of "rewritten" copies of itself.

With particularly painful/traumatic events--or, as you said, when your current reality feels unbearable --people often get stuck in a loop of rumination or re-experiencing the traumatic event. Clark is continuously ruminating over the dissolution of his relationship, replaying the arguments over and over, sometimes substituting new outcomes, hence the ultra-distorted, humanoid copies of his ex-wife and the monstrous version of himself (I believe he even says this in the dining room scene).

What solidified this reading for me was the detail that ASYNC used to make MRI machines. An MRI creates a picture of the brain...and now the ASYCN researchers are mapping the Backrooms.
2. I mean I'd say it has "too much story". Clearly the screenwriter or A24 felt the idea of exploring the Backrooms wasn't enough so they had to shoehorn in some generic character drama
  - As opposed to? 2 hours of liminal spaces with a stick monster chasing? Theres plenty of that content already
3. Backrooms was enjoyable, but it definitely had some major issues, which I’m willing to bet largely stem from Kane making the leap from YouTube to the big screen (a lot of other directors of the same background have similar issues with their debut efforts, but him directly adapting his own series probably made it more noticeable).

**Body:** I, more or less spontaneously, decided to see Digger in the theater last night. I left at the end rather psyched on it. I'm happy this movie exists and I think more people should see it.

That said, I've noticed that even among those who appreciated the film, my thoughts and feelings tend to diverge on the matter of what its true intent was.

I didn't find it to be a cynical, doomer film. Actually I found it rather becalming, the more it sussed itself out in my head. It's not so much pointing a finger at the audience, but rather poses some simple, sobering, important questions: Is it enough to be angry with the state of the world? Are you satisfied simply knowing who is to blame? Is the media we absorb acting in favor of our expansion into higher perspectives, or is it just "giving us what we want" with figures we love to hate and issues we love to fret over?

I'm not sure if it's about climate change as much as it's about our modern eco-system of thoughts and attitudes that revolve around a sense of limitation and powerlessness about the madness of our moment. The film compellingly suggests that we are baiting ourselves with a promise of catharsis by identifying the enemy and exposing it to its barest presentation, to finally laugh at it and celebrate its death, when really it's all just part of the dysfunctional turning world. It's a point of challenge that this came out around the same time as the Musk documentary, as well as the Elizabeth Holmes movie with Nathan Fielder.

If the play within the movie was actually funny and entertaining, this message would not have been emphasized. It would have been thought of as a good comedy with a message at the end. It's asking us all, what are we really doing here? Having an opinion because we think that's how we should show up? Are we going to stick and react to the cultural grid of collective perception forever?

Can we hold and regard our experience in a new way? 

Did anyone else feel the sky at the very end?

I do think people who loved this movie likely did pick up on this interpretation, after all it's not particularly subtle about it when the moment comes. I'm just adding my voice to the choir that this is a very thoughtful and worthwhile film, especially for those, like Innaritu would seem to be, who are bored with the ideological gridlock, fear, rage and powerlessness we have perpetuated to eachother and demanded from media in so many ways.

## 5. Full Metal Jacket: Is This Movie Due For A Re-Appraisal?

**Score:** 13
**Body:** Is Full Metal Jacket now Kubrick’s most misunderstood film?  Does it deserve more appreciation, or is it still too little too late?   

When I was a kid, I used to love Roger Ebert’s reviews.  Today, it seems that most people still agree with Mr. Ebert: that the Parris Island sequence is stunning, but the rest of the movie falls apart.  

To admit my own bias, one of my favourite movies is Eyes Wide Shut. It’s not entertaining in the usual way, but it’s such a re-watchable, engrossing movie. When Kubrick’s final movie came out, it had a polarized reception like most of Kubrick’s movies.  And like most Kubrick movies, it seems to be appreciated a lot more today.

It got me wondering, don’t I undervalue Full Metal Jacket?  Honestly, it’s still a pretty hard movie to wrap my head around.  

I mean this in a loving way, but with Full Metal Jacket, the ‘film-bros’ seem to argue with the ‘normies’ a lot. Duality of man, man. We all have an inner film-bro and inner normie.

The film-bros point out things like:

\- It is important to recognize that Full Metal Jacket is actually 3 acts, not 2 halves. Each act is pretty much 40 minutes and segues mi gusta in a clean way:  

* Act 1: Parris Island, from Hartman choking Pyle to Pyle shooting Hartman, and that cold, cold blue light that fades to black  
*  Act 2: Stars and Stripes, from Joker taking pictures of the prostitute with his camera, to the squad pushing another prostitute into an abandoned movie theater - fade to black again
* Act 3: The Sniper, which is characterized from start to end by the redness of fires, from the rabbit-toy explosion to Joker shooting the girl, before the flame-licked Mickey Mouse March (and don’t forget ‘Paint it Black’ in the credits!)

\- Or to put it in a more substantive way:

* Act 1: The soldiers are trained by the rough-talking sergeant. The innocent Pyle is broken down and degraded until he turns ‘shadow’, taking vengeance against the sergeant.    
* Act 2: The trained soldiers go to war against another country. We first see the degradation of its people in the female prostitute, but then there are countless horrors. With the journalists and film crew, this section has a big focus on winning ‘hearts and minds’.
*  Act 3: A teenage girl, an innocent in the degradation of her country, has become a killer herself, wreaking vengeance against the soldiers. Then, when the girl begs to be shot, the same sound cue plays as when Pyle shoots himself.  Joker killing the child may be an act of mercy, but he’s turned ‘shadow’ as well.  
*  ‘Paint It Black’ Credits: Fuck. Look at what we’ve done, all of us as people /  But fk, isn’t this pretty rock ‘n roll?      

They also say stuff like: 

* Give Stanley some credit:  he was very knowledgable about war. More than half his movies are about it.  Might he be saying something worthwhile about Vietnam, or modern warfare, or the nature of war itself?
* The bombed out city was actually period-accurate to the real destruction in Hué. People are just yearning to see the exoticism of jungles, not the uncomfortable reality of a city that could’ve been much like yours or mine   

In turn, where I think the connoisseurs can be condescending and don’t give the main audience enough slack:

* After ‘Barry Lyndon’,  Kubrick’s movies are genuinely weird and puzzling. E.g. Jonathon Rosenbaum called him the ‘Great Confounder’.  He said Kubrick’s movies weren’t cold but actually full of emotions . . . it’s just that the emotions were “convoluted and elusive”. I’ve noticed the line readings become less conventional and somewhat defamiliarizing: think of that scene wherein Dick Halloran explains the Shining, the gay hotel clerk in Eyes Wide Shut, or the affected delivery that young soldiers in Full Metal announce their dumb, trauma-bonding jokes  
* For Full Metal specifically, the use of language is so crass to hear, but at its brisk pace, the movie doesn’t really stop and invite you to reflect how the grotesquerie of the language shapes the soldiers. It’s a big part of the movie, yet it’s under-discussed with no consensus about what it’s doing, that the language seems to have some sort of disturbing logic in its application.  
* The movie is very lean, but not at all as accessible as Paths of Glory or Fear and Desire.  Maybe it’s so lean that all the elements have to be telegraphed more eloquently, and Kubrick couldn’t control everything to his liking. For example, he actually did create a jungle set - it just wasn’t convincing enough to him. Then he had to shoot the Vietnam scenes before the Parris Island ones, not by choice. And he wasn’t sure how to end the movie himself.

My own take is that Full Metal Jacket is a very thoughtful, anti-war movie. Whether intended or not, Kubrick’s movies were much more moralistic after Clockwork Orange. With Animal Mother, I suspect an intention to show how killing one’s enemies can be heroic or exciting, and in Cowboy’s death, the pathos of friends holding a dead comrade.  **But this is always accompanied by the trauma of losing one’s mind:**  **for the soldiers to function, they have to be thinking yet somehow anti-rational, regressively broken down into weird, infant-men lacking innocence - born again,** **born hard**.

What do you guys think? After what we get in Parris Island, are the yuk-yuks more of a bug than a feature? Are the three acts knotted together well enough? Compared to other well-known movies, do we under-rate what Full Metal Jacket has to convey about war? It’s been almost 40 years since this movie came out, and a little more than 50 years since the end of the Vietnam War. As before, so today. They cover our eyes, but we already know.
